qs.q: A patient living in a rural endemic area presents with spiking fevers, hepatosplenomegaly, and severe cachexia (Kala-azar). What type of cellular parasitism is characteristic of the causative agent?
o: Extracellular hemoflagellate residing freely in blood
Obligate intracellular parasite of reticuloendothelial cells
Facultative intracellular parasite within skeletal muscle
Intranuclear parasite infecting mature circulating erythrocytes
Coelozoic parasite inhabiting the large vascular lumens
qs.e: Leishmania species are obligate intracellular protozoa residing inside macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system.
qs.s: Weekly Year 2: Parasitology Exam - November 6, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A patient returning from a tropical region presents with irregular fever spikes, splenomegaly, and dark hyperpigmented skin patches (Kala-azar). Within which specific host cellular compartment do the causative hemoflagellates replicate?
o: Endosomal vacuoles of macrophages in tissues
Extracellular blood plasma spaces in circulation
Cytosol of skeletal muscle fibers through body
Lumen of renal collecting ducts in the kidney
Endothelial lining of brain capillaries in CNS
qs.e: Leishmania species are obligate intracellular parasites that replicate within the phagolysosomes of macrophages.

qs.q: What is a common clinical feature observed in East African patients who develop Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL)?
o: Universal requirement for prolonged intravenous amphotericin B
Exclusive involvement of the central nervous system
Rapid progression to visceral organ failure within weeks
Majority of patients experience spontaneous healing
qs.e: In East Africa, a majority of patients with Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis experience spontaneous healing, unlike Indian cases which are typically treated with pentavalent antimonials for 60–120 days.

qs.q: What clinical feature characterizes Post Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) after treatment for visceral leishmaniasis?
o: Acute renal failure and massive hepatosplenomegaly
Deep necrotic ulcers with raised borders on limbs
Hypopigmented macules, papules, or nodules on skin
High-grade fever with rigors and severe pancytopenia
qs.e: PKDL typically manifests as hypopigmented macules, papules, or nodules occurring concurrently with or after the cure of visceral leishmaniasis. It does not present with the acute systemic fevers characteristic of primary VL.

qs.q: A patient with post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) presents with erythematous patches distributed in a characteristic pattern on the face. What is this facial distribution pattern typically called?
o: Heliotrope distribution
V-sign distribution
Butterfly distribution
Malar rash
qs.e: PKDL erythematous patches on the face characteristically present in a butterfly distribution. A malar rash is classically associated with systemic lupus erythematosus rather than this parasitic skin condition.

qs.q: What is the typical incubation period for Kala-azar before clinical symptoms begin to manifest insidiously in an infected individual?
o: 2 to 6 months
3 to 5 years
1 to 2 weeks
6 to 12 months
qs.e: The incubation period for Kala-azar typically ranges from 2 to 6 months, though it can occasionally span from 10 days to 2 years. Untreated cases lead to fatality within two years due to opportunistic infections.

es.q: List and explain the clinical manifestations and laboratory diagnosis of Visceral Leishmaniasis (Kala-azar).
es.m:
- **Fever and organomegaly**: Abrupt onset of moderate- to high-grade fever with rigor, chills, hepatomegaly, and a palpable spleen by the second week.
- **Systemic signs**: Weight loss, malaise, skin-dark discoloration, pedal edema, and ascites in advanced disease with hypoalbuminemia.
- **Hematologic complications**: Anemia, pancytopenia from bone marrow dysfunction, and bleeding manifestations such as epistaxis, retinal hemorrhages, and GI bleeding.
- **Gold standard diagnosis**: Demonstration of amastigotes in smears of tissue aspirates using Giemsa stain (splenic smears have >95% sensitivity).
- **Alternative diagnostics**: Bone marrow smears, lymph node aspirates, tissue cultures, ELIS

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Visceral leishmaniasis is a sand‑fly transmitted protozoal infection causing fever, weight loss, splenomegaly and pancytopenia. It is common in East Africa and other low‑resource settings, often co‑existing with HIV or malnutrition.

sections.p: Visceral leishmaniasis (VL) is infection of the reticulo‑endothelial system by Leishmania donovani complex, presenting with prolonged fever, weight loss, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly and pancytopenia.
b: Diagnosis requires demonstration of the parasite in tissue (splenic, bone‑marrow or lymph‑node aspirate) or a positive rK39 rapid test in endemic areas.

t.b: Confirms exposure; a positive result in a febrile patient with splenomegaly strongly supports VL
Highly sensitive; useful for relapse or PKDL when microscopy not feasible

sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical and laboratory parameters: degree of splenomegaly, hemoglobin level, platelet count and presence of co‑infection.
b: Mild: Hb ≥ 9 g/dL, platelets ≥ 100 × 10⁹/L, spleen < 5 cm below costal margin.
Moderate: Hb 7‑8 g/dL, platelets 50‑99 × 10⁹/L, spleen 5‑10 cm.
Severe: Hb < 7 g/dL, platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L, spleen > 10 cm, or organ failure.

sections.p: VL is caused by Leishmania donovani complex transmitted by female Phlebotomus sandflies. In East Africa, co‑factors that increase risk include HIV infection, malnutrition, and prior kala‑azar episodes.
b: Leishmania donovani infection (primary cause).
HIV co‑infection – accelerates disease and hampers treatment response.
Severe malnutrition – impairs cell‑mediated immunity.
Concurrent infections (TB, malaria, bacterial sepsis) that further depress marrow function.

sections.p: Patients develop a prolonged (weeks‑months) fever, marked weight loss, anorexia, and progressive enlargement of spleen and liver. Laboratory shows pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemia and elevated ESR.
b: Fever often irregular, spikes in the evening.
Splenomegaly is usually massive and may cause early satiety.
Pancytopenia leads to fatigue, easy bruising and susceptibility to bacterial infections.

sections.p: Investigations focus on confirming the parasite, assessing disease burden and ruling out co‑morbidities.

t.b: Detects pancytopenia; severe anemia or thrombocytopenia guides transfusion need
Identify hepatic involvement; transaminases may be mildly raised
Screens for TB or pneumonia, common co‑infections in low‑resource settings
Provides definitive parasite detection; also evaluates marrow cellularity
Detects co‑infection that alters treatment duration and prognosis

sections.p: Complications arise from organ infiltration, immune suppression and treatment toxicity.
b: Splenic rupture – sudden abdominal pain, shock; surgical emergency.
Severe pancytopenia – life‑threatening bleeding or sepsis.
Post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) – nodular skin lesions that act as reservoirs.
HIV‑VL co‑infection – rapid deterioration, higher relapse risk.

sections.p: First‑line therapy is a single‑dose liposomal amphotericin B where available; otherwise, sodium stibogluconate or miltefosine are used with close monitoring.
b: Supportive care: blood transfusion for Hb < 7 g/dL, platelet transfusion if < 20 × 10⁹/L with bleeding, nutritional rehabilitation.
Treat co‑infections (e.g., TB, HIV) concurrently according to local guidelines.

sections.p: Patients are reviewed weekly during treatment, then monthly for six months to detect relapse or PKDL.
b: Repeat CBC at each visit to monitor marrow recovery.
rK39 or PCR at 3 months to confirm parasitological cure.
Educate on vector control: insecticide‑treated nets, indoor residual spraying.
Screen household contacts for early detection.

sections.p: Conditions that also cause massive splenomegaly and pancytopenia.
b: Malaria (especially chronic Plasmodium falciparum).
Typhoid fever with splenic involvement.
Brucellosis.
Hematologic malignancies (e.g., lymphoma).

sections.p: Certain tests may be falsely negative or non‑specific in endemic settings.
b: rK39 may be negative early in disease; rely on tissue microscopy if suspicion remains.
Peripheral smear can miss low‑level parasitemia; bone‑marrow aspirate is more sensitive.
Elevated ESR is non‑specific; do not use it to stage disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden abdominal pain with hypotension (possible splenic rupture).
Bleeding gums or petechiae with platelets < 20 × 10⁹/L.
High‑grade fever unresponsive to antibiotics suggesting uncontrolled VL.

faq.q: Why is splenomegaly so prominent in VL?
faq.a: Leishmania parasites proliferate in macrophages of the reticulo‑endothelial system, causing hyperplasia of splenic tissue.

faq.q: Can VL be cured without amphotericin?
faq.a: Yes, sodium stibogluconate or miltefosine are effective alternatives, though cure rates are lower and toxicity higher.

faq.q: What is PKDL and why does it matter?
faq.a: Post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis is a skin manifestation after treatment that can harbor parasites and sustain transmission.

exam: A 32‑year‑old farmer from rural Kenya presents with 3 weeks of fever, weight loss and a 12 cm splenomegaly. Which diagnostic test gives the quickest bedside confirmation and why? — rK39 rapid test; it is cheap, gives results in 15 minutes and has high sensitivity in endemic areas.

Your patient with confirmed VL is HIV‑positive and CD4 count 150. How does this affect your treatment plan? — Extend amphotericin course to 10 days or use combination therapy; monitor for relapse and start antiretroviral therapy after VL control.

During treatment with sodium stibogluconate the patient develops a rising serum amylase and epigastric pain. What is the likely complication and what should you do? — Pancreatitis; stop stibogluconate and switch to liposomal amphotericin if available.
A child with VL shows platelets of 15 × 10⁹/L and active gum bleeding. What immediate step is required? — Transfuse platelets and consider urgent splenic protection measures.

How would you differentiate VL from chronic malaria when both cause splenomegaly and anemia? — Malaria shows periodic fever spikes, positive thick smear, and responds to antimalarials; VL has persistent fever, pancytopenia, and positive rK39 or tissue microscopy.

Explain why post‑kala‑azar dermal leishmaniasis is a public health concern even after successful treatment. — Skin lesions contain viable parasites that can be taken up by sandflies, perpetuating transmission.
What red‑flag sign would prompt immediate surgical consultation in a VL patient? — Signs of splenic rupture: sudden left‑upper‑quadrant pain, hypotension, and peritoneal signs.
